title: Ines and the Ledger
premise: In 1899 New York, Rosalind Vasquez serves as driver and confidante to suffragist leader Adeline Hart, quietly reading the movement's letters and memorizing what powerful men would rather forget. When a census taker's probing questions expose that Rosalind is the unacknowledged daughter of a judge whose fortune bankrolls the cause, she becomes a liability to allies and a target of enemies determined to bury her claim. Racing to enter her father's hidden ledger into the public record before the century turns, Rosalind must choose between protecting Adeline, whom she loves, and telling a truth that could destroy the movement's funding. She testifies at last, wins recognition of her name if not her inheritance, and begins the new century as a witness rather than a ghost.
about_author: Mara Iversen is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing suffrage-era correspondence in upstate New York. She writes historical fiction about the women history filed under 'assistant.'

chapters.title: The Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A routine census visit to the Hart house turns sharp when the taker asks about her parentage. Rosalind deflects, but the encounter rattles her carefully maintained invisibility. Emotional beat: the first crack in a life built on being unreadable.

chapters.title: Letters Before Delivery
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, flashback woven through present. We learn how she reads the movement's mail, memorizing names, debts, and promises. Her loyalty to Adeline is absolute—and built on secrets kept for her. Beat: intimacy shadowed by transgression.

chapters.title: Judge Vasquez's Ledger
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Sorting her late mother's trunk, she finds a ledger in her father Judge Edmund Vasquez's hand: payments, land deeds, and a line acknowledging 'my daughter R.' Beat: grief colliding with sudden, dangerous hope.

chapters.title: The Driver's Silence
chapters.summary: Adeline's POV. Adeline notices Rosalind distracted after the census visit and wonders what the girl knows about the judge whose money sustains their headquarters. Beat: affection strained by the politics of not asking.

chapters.title: A Man from the Census Bureau
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The census taker returns off-duty, revealing he was hired by the Vasquez estate's lawyers to find 'undocumented heirs' before probate closes. Beat: fear sharpening into resolve—she has until December 31.

chapters.title: What the Movement Owes
chapters.summary: Treasurer's clerk POV. Inside campaign finances, we see how much of the suffrage war chest traces to Judge Vasquez—and how badly the books would survive scrutiny. Beat: institutional rot glimpsed from within.

chapters.title: Reading Adeline's Mail
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A letter reveals Adeline knew of the ledger years ago and chose silence to protect funding. Rosalind's devotion curdles. Beat: betrayal by omission, love tested against truth.

chapters.title: The Probate Clerk
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She visits the courthouse under pretense of jury duty and learns filings close January 2. A sympathetic clerk warns her the estate's lawyers will discredit any claimant without standing. Beat: the clock made concrete.

chapters.title: An Offer of Anonymity
chapters.summary: Lawyer Hale's POV. The estate offers Rosalind money and a train ticket west in exchange for signing away any claim and her silence. Beat: temptation priced exactly at the value of her name.

chapters.title: Adeline Asks Nothing
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Adeline, sensing everything, says only 'whatever you decide, drive me Tuesday.' The restraint wounds more than anger would. Beat: love expressed as deliberate blindness.

chapters.title: The Other Daughter
chapters.summary: Half-sister Claire's POV. Legitimate daughter Claire arrives in New York, charming and ruthless, hunting the same ledger to burn it. She and Rosalind meet without either admitting knowledge. Beat: two claims, one inheritance, mutual reconnaissance.

chapters.title: Ledger, Page Forty-One
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She deciphers page forty-one: the judge recorded buying Adeline's first newspaper with hush money from a bribery scandal. The movement's founding sin is in her hands. Beat: the truth becomes a weapon she doesn't want to fire.

chapters.title: Fire Drill
chapters.summary: Headquarters volunteer POV. A suspicious small fire damages the records room; the ledger's existence is now known beyond the family. Beat: escalation—the secret is no longer containable by anyone.

chapters.title: Confession on the Road
chapters.summary: Dual POV, alternating. Driving Adeline to a rally, Rosalind finally tells her everything. Adeline admits she suspected; both women grieve the years of polite lies. Beat: honesty as an act of love, costly and relieving.

chapters.title: Claire's Countermove
chapters.summary: Claire's POV. Claire files first, painting Rosalind as a servant forging documents, and leaks word to the press that the suffrage movement is entangled in scandal. Beat: the victors' historians begin writing early.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Reads
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind realizes her years of reading letters make her the only person alive who can corroborate the ledger line by line. She engages a young lawyer, Miss Okafor, willing to take an unwinnable case. Beat: invisibility reframed as expertise.

chapters.title: Pressure on the Movement
chapters.summary: Adeline's POV. Donors threaten withdrawal unless Adeline disavows Rosalind publicly. Adeline drafts the statement, then burns it. Beat: duty and love forced onto the same scale.

chapters.title: December 29
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Eve of filing, Claire offers partnership—split the estate, bury the scandal page. Rosalind refuses: the record matters more than the money. Beat: the theme stated plainly and paid for.

chapters.title: On the Record
chapters.summary: Climax. Courtroom and pressroom intercut. Rosalind files the full ledger, testifying to the scandal page alongside her own legitimacy, refusing to trade one truth for another. Beat: courage as completeness—she tells all of it or none of it counts.

chapters.title: What the Victors Write
chapters.summary: Journalist POV. Papers split: some mock 'the chauffeur heiress,' one prints the scandal. Adeline reads every version aloud to Rosalind, laughing and crying. Beat: vindication arriving imperfect, public, and shared.

chapters.title: The Inheritance That Stays
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Judgment: her name entered in the family register, the estate largely lost to legal fees, the scandal page sealed but archived. Adeline asks her to stay—not as a driver, but as the movement's keeper of records. Beat: redefinition of inheritance as witness-bearing.

chapters.title: First Entry, New Century
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, epilogue. On January 1, 1900, Rosalind opens a fresh ledger of her own and writes the first line of a true history. Beat: quiet triumph—the invisible woman becomes the one who remembers everyone.
